title: Mom's Famous Potato Soup
subtitle: thick, creamy and cheesy — loaded with bacon, cheddar and sour cream
imageAlt: Bowl of creamy potato soup topped with cheddar, crispy bacon and sour cream
servingsNote: dinner for one big eater + one hungry eater, plus 2 lunches

breakdown: Old cheddar, 2 cups shredded (½ of a 400 g block)

beforeYouStart.text: Use your biggest pot (5–6 L / Dutch oven) — 3 lb of potatoes plus broth fills it up.
Cut the potatoes the same size (about 2 cm / ¾") so they all get tender at the same time.
Shred the cheddar yourself and set the cream on the counter now — room-temp dairy melts in smoothly instead of clumping.

items.name: shredded old cheddar
items.note: 1 cup stirred in, 1 cup on top

steps.title: Crisp the bacon
steps.text: Cook the bacon in your big pot over medium, turning, until crisp — about 8–10 minutes (or air-fry at 190°C / 375°F for 8–10 min). Move to a paper towel, then crumble. Pour off all but about 1 tbsp of the fat. (Skipping bacon? Just start at step 2.)

steps.title: Soften the onion
steps.text: Add the butter to the pot over medium. When it melts, add the onion and a pinch of salt and cook, stirring, until soft and see-through but not browned, 5–6 minutes. Add the garlic for the last minute.

steps.title: Toast the flour
steps.text: Sprinkle the flour over the onions and stir for 1 minute so it coats everything and loses its raw taste.

steps.title: Add broth and potatoes
steps.text: Slowly pour in the broth while stirring, scraping up the bottom of the pot. Add the potatoes, salt, pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, thyme and paprika. Turn the heat to high and bring to a boil.

steps.title: Simmer until tender
steps.text: Turn down to medium-low, partly cover and simmer, stirring now and then so nothing sticks, until a fork slides through the potatoes with no resistance — about 15–20 minutes.

steps.title: Mash it thick
steps.text: Turn the heat off. Mash about half the potatoes right in the pot with a potato masher, leaving plenty of chunks. (Like it smoother? Use an immersion blender for a few pulses — don't over-blend or it turns gluey.)

steps.title: Make it creamy
steps.text: Turn the heat to low. Stir in the cream or milk and warm 2–3 minutes — don't let it boil. Take the pot off the heat and stir in 1 cup of the cheddar, a handful at a time, until melted. Taste and add more salt and pepper until it's well seasoned.

steps.title: Load it up and serve
steps.text: Ladle into bowls and top each with the rest of the cheddar, crumbled bacon and a spoonful of sour cream.

fixIt.fix: Mash more of the potatoes, or simmer uncovered 5 minutes on low, stirring. A handful of extra cheddar thickens it too.
Stir in broth or milk, ¼ cup at a time. It thickens a lot in the fridge, so leftovers always need a splash.
It almost always needs more salt — add ¼ tsp at a time and taste. A knob of butter or a bit more garlic powder helps too.
The soup was too hot when the cheese went in. Next time take it off the heat first and add it a handful at a time. Pre-shredded bags melt less smoothly than a block you shred.
It boiled after the dairy went in. It still tastes fine — keep it on low from now on. Cream holds up better than milk.
Don't scrape the burnt bit up. Pour the soup into a clean pot and keep the heat lower, stirring more often.

saleTip: A 10 lb bag of russets is often $5–7 at No Frills — much cheaper per pound than the 5 lb bag. Bacon and block cheddar both go on sale often (bacon ~2 for $9–10, cheddar ~$5–6 per 400 g) — stock up and freeze the bacon.
swap: Use whole milk instead of cream to save about $2 (just keep it on low), or leave out the bacon for a meat-free night.
leftovers: Fridge up to 4 days in sealed containers — great for lunch. Freezes for 2 months (it can get a little grainy; whisk well while reheating). Reheat gently on low with a splash of milk — don't boil.
source: Mom's recipe, with steps based on classic loaded baked potato soup (America's Test Kitchen, Once Upon a Chef)
doneness: Potatoes break apart when pressed against the pot with a spoon; bacon is crisp. Reheat leftovers to 74°C (165°F).
gear: Large pot or Dutch oven (5–6 L)
prepAhead: Peel and cube the potatoes up to a day ahead — keep them covered in cold water in the fridge.
Cook and crumble the bacon ahead; refrigerate up to 4 days.
Shred the cheddar and dice the onion the night before.
reheat: Stovetop: low heat with a splash of milk or broth, stirring, until steaming (74°C / 165°F) — don't boil. Microwave: 1 min at a time, stirring between. Add fresh toppings after reheating.
story: This is Mom's soup — the one that showed up on cold nights and sick days, and always tasted like home. Thick, buttery and loaded with cheddar and bacon. Tap edit to add the story in your own words.

basic.note: Mom's soup with the essentials: potatoes, broth, milk and cheddar. Still thick and cosy.

stepNotes.0: Basic: no bacon — skip this step.
stepNotes.6: Basic: milk instead of cream — keep it on low.
stepNotes.7: Basic: top with the rest of the cheddar.

fancy.note: Loaded and silky: cream, aged cheddar, crisp bacon, a swirl of sour cream and crispy potato skins on top.

items.name: shredded aged white cheddar
items.note: stirred in with the old cheddar

items.name: bacon
items.note: extra, for thick crumbles on top

stepNotes.6: Fancy: stir the aged white cheddar in with the first cup of old cheddar.

addSteps.title: Fancy finish
addSteps.text: Ladle into warm bowls. Add a spoon of sour cream, then drag a spoon through it for a swirl. Pile big bacon crumbles and cheddar in the centre and finish with cracked black pepper and a pinch of paprika.

plating: Warm the bowls with hot water first so the soup stays hot.
Sour cream swirl, then toppings piled in the centre — not scattered.
A tiny pinch of paprika for colour.

why.0-3: Flour is what makes it thick and silky. Skip it and mash more potato instead.
why.0-6: Cream makes it rich. Milk works but keep it on low so it doesn't curdle.
why.1-0: Cheddar is the flavour and the thickness at the end — don't skip it.
why.0-4: Broth is the backbone of the flavour. Water works in a pinch with extra salt.

funFact: Prince Edward Island, Canada’s smallest province, grows roughly a quarter of all the potatoes in the country.

keeps.note: the potatoes turn grainy and the cream can split

pairs: Soup and sandwich night — make the Philly while the soup simmers
